topic: How does a cat always land on its feet? (the righting reflex)
script:
Your cat can do a flip that baffled scientists in 1894.
Falling upside down, with nothing to push against,
it still turns over.
So how?
First, its inner ear senses which way is down.
Then it bends in the middle,
like two cats glued together.
It tucks its front legs in,
so the front half spins fast,
while the stretched back legs barely turn.
Then it swaps,
and the back half catches up.
A bendy spine and a loose collarbone make it possible,
all in under a second.
Kittens master it by about seven weeks.
So, have you ever seen your cat pull off the flip?
key_facts: Etienne-Jules Marey's 1894 chronophotographs of a falling cat puzzled the French Academy of Sciences, since the cat turned with no external push
The vestibular system in the inner ear tells the cat which way is up
The cat bends at the middle and rotates front and back halves separately: tucked legs spin fast, extended legs slowly (tuck-and-turn), then it swaps
A very flexible backbone and no functional (free-floating) collarbone help
The righting reflex appears at 3-4 weeks and is perfected by about 7 weeks
